title: Following the Trail of Data

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is the cover; page 2 is Summary Statement; pages 3-4 are Executive Summary; page 5 is contents; pages 6-26 are the main paper; pages 27-32 are appendix data and model plots; page 33 is references.

notes: All 33 text pages and all 33 rendered pages were reviewed in order.
Eight model-visible contact proxies stayed below 450000 bytes; three independent page-range audits checked formulas, pseudocode, tables, plot labels, and original-paper defects.

context_sources.summary: Behavioral and geographic-profiling literature motivates circle, distance-decay, buffer-zone, and human-bias claims.
GoogleEarth and CommunityWalk are named as sources for the five-offender coordinate-time appendix.
Eleven references cover environmental criminology, serial-offender behavior, functional distance measures, CrimeStat, and bounded rationality.

inputs: locations and dates of crimes believed to belong to one offender
candidate search grid and optional buffer
decisions: whether the offender geometry and data quality make the method usable

section_map.summary: The cover identifies the decision-oriented title, control number, and submission date without adding unsupported claims.

The Summary moves from police inputs and two prediction targets to additive distance-decay fields, virtual-crime scoring, time extrapolation, time coupling, two metrics, a Sutcliffe result, and color-map output.

The two-page letter translates required inputs, probability-map outputs, single-offender and single-base assumptions, commuter and geography exclusions, function flexibility, runtime, color bands, and police actions into decision language.
The contents exposes a background-problem-assumptions-metrics-functions-algorithms-results-conclusion-future-research-appendix route.

The background motivates computation through human judgment bias, defines the serial-killer scope, distinguishes nearby categories, supplies behavioral evidence, and introduces circle, distance-decay, and buffer-zone mechanisms.
The problem section reduces the police request to predicting one base, the next crime location, and its time, then states the color-priority and bilinear-interpolation handoff.

The assumptions section fixes single-offender linkage, one base, circle-like coverage, stable distance decay, noncommuter behavior, and homogeneous terrain, population, and opportunity while naming future relaxations.
The metric section defines weighted mean center, minimum-distance center, standard-deviational circle, and standard-deviational ellipse as global spatial summaries.
Four synthetic point layouts establish expected home and next-event behavior before formal modeling: uniform fill, square outline, linear spread, and two clusters.
Five distance-decay families are compared by their near-scene behavior, buffer-zone interpretation, cutoff or tail behavior, and crime-type adaptability.

The criminal-location method replaces a single center with a grid distribution formed by additive distance contributions, normalization, prioritized search, automatic hotspots, and interchangeable kernels.

The next-crime method inserts a virtual event at each candidate, recomputes the home field, scores squared distribution change, adds an edge buffer, and discusses quartic cost, caching, and parallelization.
The time section withholds the last event, extrapolates an average interval, compares predicted and actual Chester Turner timing, and chooses a restrained linear rule over strong-end alternatives.
The coupling section defines a decreasing recency weight, inserts it into both spatial algorithms, and contrasts correlated with uncorrelated synthetic time assignments through six heat maps.

The results define straight-line error and ranked-grid search cost, withhold the most recent crime, compare five kernels with and without time coupling for Sutcliffe and Turner, and report exact paired values.

The conclusion separates favorable clustered Sutcliffe behavior from displaced-hub Turner failure, explains why next-crime prediction can outperform home prediction, and admits that time coupling often worsened performance.
Future work maps omitted terrain, population, social geography, opportunity, and personality traits to optional features and parameter changes.
The appendix preserves predicted-versus-actual dates and a five-offender latitude-longitude-time table with source attribution and visible chronology defects.

The plot appendix places home and next-crime heat maps for five kernels and a time-weighted variant on common coordinates, while page 32 exposes a duplicated and mislabeled Sutcliffe pair under a Chester Turner heading.

Eleven references connect geographic profiling, environmental criminology, serial-offender behavior, journey-to-crime decay, mapping, and bounded rationality, with several bibliographic defects retained.

assumptions.summary: All events supplied in one run belong to one criminal.
The criminal operates from exactly one home base.
A circle-like region around the most separated crimes plausibly contains the base.
Stable offenders exhibit distance decay and commuter offenders are outside the current scope.
Terrain, population density, opportunity, and habitability are homogeneous.
Latitude and longitude can be handled through the paper's planar distance calculations.
Additive noncanceling distance contributions produce a useful relative residence field.
A candidate next crime is likely when its insertion changes the residence field only slightly.
Recent crimes deserve more weight when behavior or location changes over time.
Synthetic correlated and uncorrelated assignments reveal when time coupling is useful.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Input locations and times are treated as linked to one offender and mapped to a colored rectangular grid.
Population, opportunity, terrain, roads, and habitability are omitted rather than encoded as covariates or masks.
The continuous search region is discretized into n by m grid lines and evaluated cell by cell.
An augmented domain is introduced to reduce candidate edge artifacts, although its size and candidate loop are inconsistent.
The most recent event is removed before home and next-crime evaluation.
Appendix A provides 52 latitude-longitude-date rows across Sutcliffe, Turner, Zodiac, Grim Sleeper, and Jack the Ripper.

models.summary: The weighted coordinate center interface retains weighted mean center: Summarize crime locations through a possibly weighted coordinate center.
The geometric median objective interface retains minimum-distance center: Choose the point with minimum total Euclidean distance to all scenes.
The compact-support linear kernel interface retains linear distance decay: Decrease influence linearly to a finite cutoff.
The buffer-peaked normal kernel interface retains normal distance decay: Represent a preferred travel radius or buffer-zone peak.
The monotone exponential kernel interface retains negative exponential decay: Assign maximum influence at a scene and decay monotonically with distance.
The rise-then-decay kernel interface retains truncated negative exponential decay: Create a linearly rising buffer-zone branch followed by exponential decay.
The plateau-then-decay kernel interface retains plateaued negative exponential decay: Keep constant cell influence inside a radius and decay outside it.
The additive distance field interface retains criminal location raw field: Accumulate noncanceling contributions from all known crime locations.
The normalized grid field interface retains criminal location normalization: Normalize the grid score so all displayed values sum to one.
The rectangular-grid work interface retains criminal location runtime: Count one kernel evaluation per grid point and known crime.
The square-grid approximation interface retains square-grid runtime approximation: Explain the paper's simplified home-field complexity claim.
The candidate-event insertion interface retains virtual crime augmentation: Create one hypothetical next crime for each candidate point.
The candidate-conditioned home field interface retains virtual criminal field: Recompute the normalized home field after inserting a candidate event.
The sum-squared field change interface retains distribution deviation score: Measure how surprising a candidate event is relative to the original home field.
The normalized deviation field interface retains paper next-crime normalization: Retain the paper's returned normalized deviation field for auditing its score direction.
The nested candidate-grid work interface retains next-crime runtime: Count one square-grid home-field recomputation for every square-grid candidate.
The average-span extrapolation interface retains future crime time extrapolation: Predict the withheld final event time from the observed span.
The decreasing recency weight interface retains time weighting function: Give more recent events larger weight while approaching a lower asymptote.
The time-weighted additive field interface retains weighted criminal raw field: Multiply every crime's distance contribution by a recency weight.
The normalized time-weighted field interface retains weighted field normalization: Return a normalized recency-weighted criminal-location field.
The straight-line point error interface retains error distance: Measure how far the highest-scored location lies from the known target.
The ranked grid fraction interface retains search cost: Measure the fraction of higher-priority grid cells searched before the true cell.
Use the two most separated crimes to motivate a bounded residence region before applying finer ranking.
Compare uniform, boundary, linear, and clustered point patterns with expected centers, spread, and next-event regions.
Iterate every grid point, add all distance-kernel contributions, normalize the field, and return it.
Freeze the original home field, insert one candidate crime at a time, recompute, measure squared change, and rank candidates.
Reuse the contribution of the original N crimes and combine only the new virtual point before renormalization.
Multiply each crime contribution by a decreasing age weight and repeat both home and next-crime calculations.
Generate near-linear locations, assign Poisson times monotonically or randomly, and compare weighted with unweighted heat maps.
Remove the most recent crime, run five kernels with and without time coupling, and score home and next-crime outputs by distance and search cost.
Contrast clustered Sutcliffe success with displaced-hub Turner failure and preserve separate conclusions for home and next-crime prediction.

dependency_graph.handoff: The center and spread summaries are checked against intuitive point layouts.
A selected distance kernel supplies every crime-to-grid contribution.
The raw summed field is normalized for map display and ranking.
The original home field is the reference for every virtual-crime candidate.
Every candidate-conditioned field is compared pointwise with the frozen reference.
The paper normalizes the deviation values, creating the score-direction inconsistency retained in the warning pass.
Event age scales each distance-kernel contribution.
The weighted raw field is normalized on the augmented domain.
Weighted and unweighted fields are contrasted under controlled time-location association.
Error distance scores both home and next-crime maxima.
Search cost converts field ranking into a resource-oriented metric.
Exact paired values support separate Sutcliffe and Turner conclusions.

verification.summary: Four synthetic point layouts state expected center, spread, cluster, and next-event behavior before the algorithm is accepted.
verification.strength: Creates qualitative invariants for later fields.
verification.limitation: No numeric acceptance criteria or repeated perturbation study is provided.

verification.summary: Figure 1 places four displayed kernels on common distance and unnormalized-score axes.
verification.strength: Makes near-scene and tail assumptions visually comparable.
verification.limitation: The plateaued kernel is discussed but omitted from the legend.

verification.summary: A two-cluster example produces two hotspots without an external clustering method.
verification.strength: Demonstrates a positive structural property of the additive field.
verification.limitation: The example is qualitative and contains an unresolved left/right editing placeholder.

verification.summary: No-buffer and 30-percent-buffer fields are shown side by side.
verification.strength: Visually demonstrates the reason for evaluating a larger domain.
verification.limitation: Program 2 instead states 40 percent and loops candidates over the buffer.

verification.summary: Correlated and uncorrelated time assignments are compared with and without weighting.
verification.strength: Isolates whether time-location association changes the field.
verification.limitation: Seeds, parameters, repetitions, and quantitative metrics are absent.

verification.summary: The latest crime is removed to emulate the information available to police before that event.
verification.strength: Prevents the withheld location from directly entering its own field.
verification.limitation: Only one origin per case is evaluated and other tuning choices are not nested.

verification.summary: Five decay functions are compared for two offenders, two targets, and coupled versus uncoupled modes using two metrics.
verification.strength: Keeps model variants under a common result table.
verification.limitation: Only two main offender cases support the exact table and no uncertainty is reported.

verification.summary: Sutcliffe and Turner are contrasted to expose clustered success and displaced-hub failure.
verification.strength: Prevents a single favorable case from defining universal performance.
verification.limitation: No pre-use diagnostic or abstention threshold is calibrated.

verification.summary: Sutcliffe home and next-crime fields are plotted for each kernel on common coordinates.
verification.strength: Allows direct qualitative comparison of hotspot movement and smoothness.
verification.limitation: No color bar, calibrated probability scale, or metric annotation appears on the maps.

verification.summary: The purported Chester Turner plot page is checked against axes and captions.
verification.strength: Detects that the expected case visual is absent rather than silently accepting the heading.
verification.limitation: The missing Turner visualization prevents visual verification of its table results.

results_trace.summary: Most kernels reportedly locate Sutcliffe after about 15 percent of the selected search area.
For Sutcliffe, the lowest reported next-crime uncoupled pair is 0.27/1.46 under negative exponential decay; coupled is 0.26/1.46.
For Turner, next-crime search costs remain about 40.68 to 45.93 while home search costs remain about 58.64 to 66.70.
Time coupling generally increases rather than decreases many home and Turner errors or search costs.
The conclusion says next-crime prediction is more accurate than home prediction and limits coupling benefits to correlated spatial-temporal behavior.

contributions.summary: Generalizes a single center into a full additive distance-decay field.
Uses the same interface to preserve clusters and permit crime-type-specific kernels.
Introduces virtual-event field stability as a next-crime heuristic.
Adds caching and grid-point parallelism to the expensive candidate loop.
Adds a recency-weight interface to adapt to behavior changes.
Uses both point error and ranked search cost to connect predictions to police resources.

writing_logic.summary: Summary chain: police task -> additive home field -> virtual-crime field -> time prediction -> coupling -> case metrics -> strongest result -> maps.
Executive chain: required inputs -> outputs -> single-offender and one-base limits -> commuter and geography limits -> flexibility -> compute time -> color-coded actions.
Background chain: human judgment bias -> operational definition -> offender behavior -> circle hypothesis -> distance decay -> buffer zone.
Formalization chain: assumptions -> centers and spread -> synthetic expectations -> distance kernels.
Home-model chain: additive pull analogy -> grid discretization -> complexity -> Program 1 -> prioritized search -> clustering -> function independence.
Next-event chain: virtual insertion -> field deviation -> edge failure -> buffer -> quartic cost -> caching -> parallel execution.
Temporal chain: withheld-time extrapolation -> restrained method choice -> recency function -> weighted algorithms -> controlled synthetic comparison.
Evaluation chain: two metrics -> latest-event holdout -> kernel and coupling matrix -> exact table -> favorable and failure cases -> deployment caution.

language_observations.summary: The summary uses one paragraph each for contract, complete method pipeline, and evidence/output.
The executive summary states limitations before strengths and ends with explicit police actions.
Definitions and exclusions narrow the population before modeling claims are introduced.
Synthetic layouts make expected model behavior inspectable before equations.
The gravitational-pull analogy explains additive fields without replacing the formal algorithm.
Computation, Pseudocode, and Why it Works form a reusable method-explanation sequence.
First, Next, We then, and This gives us create an auditable procedural chain.
Each metric is defined once and then interpreted separately for home search and future-crime prevention.
The conclusion immediately contrasts good clustered data with misleading displaced-hub data.
Future research maps each omitted context variable to optional inputs and parameter changes.

Shows directional spread and two-hotspot expectations that a credible field should preserve.

Demonstrates automatic multimodal hotspots without an external clustering stage.
Exposes the augmented grid, virtual-event loop, sum-squared deviation, and returned field.
Shows the edge artifact without a buffer and the changed field with a 30 percent buffer.
Compares the predicted withheld event in red with the actual event in black.
Shows how the time weight enters both home and future-crime algorithms.
Displays a fall from roughly 10 at day zero toward 2 by day 100.
Contrasts weighted and unweighted next-crime fields for correlated and uncorrelated synthetic timings.
Shows criminal-location fields changing less rapidly than next-crime fields under correlated motion.
Reports exact Search Cost / Error Distance pairs for five kernels, two targets, two coupling modes, and two offenders.
Displays timing error for five offenders without a caption or stated unit metric.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A compact complete pipeline plausibly improves judge traceability without proving the model correct.
Explicit pseudocode and complexity plausibly increase inspectability.
A common exact result table plausibly supports comparison, while the unreported units and uncertainty reduce credibility.

weaknesses.summary: The mean-center equations are called averages but omit division by the total weight; taking every w_i=1 yields coordinate sums rather than a center unless normalized weights are silently assumed.
The 68 percent and 95 percent SDC coverage statements require a distributional interpretation that is not derived for these spatial point patterns.
The circle-hypothesis evidence for serial rapists is generalized to serial murder and other criminal types without a direct transfer validation.
One offender and exactly one home base are assumed, excluding linkage uncertainty, multiple anchors, and mobile or commuter behavior.
Terrain, road access, population density, opportunity, and inhabitable-area constraints are omitted, so high-score cells can be operationally impossible.
Euclidean calculations on latitude and longitude are not accompanied by a projection, spherical-distance rule, or unit conversion.
Linear, Normal, exponential, truncated, and plateau kernel parameters are not reported in a reproducible calibration table.
The additive normalized field is called a criminal-location probability although no generative likelihood, prior, or calibration test supports that interpretation.
Finer meshes are said to approximate an ideal smooth solution, but no resolution sensitivity or convergence diagnostic is shown.
The concrete 2 GHz runtime and 36 by 36 meter England-grid claim has no implementation, benchmark log, memory use, or kernel specification.

The prose says lower squared distribution deviation means a more likely next crime, but Programs 2 and 3 normalize the deviation without reversing its order, so larger deviations receive larger returned values.
The prose says virtual crimes are not added in the buffer, yet Programs 2 and 3 iterate candidate g over the augmented grid G prime rather than the interior G.
Program 2 specifies a 40 percent boundary buffer, whereas Figure 3 and Program 3 use 30 percent.
The O(n^4) next-crime complexity collapses a two-dimensional n by m grid to one symbol and does not state the effect of crime count or buffer size.
The claimed factor-N caching speedup and normalization-preserving combination are not derived or benchmarked.
Near-perfect parallel speedup equal to the number of cores ignores communication, memory bandwidth, scheduling, and aggregation overhead.
With observed times t_1 through t_(N-1), the mean of the N-2 observed intervals normally has denominator N-2, not the paper's N-1.
The time method is called linear regression, but the displayed rule is a one-step average-span extrapolation with no fitted regression line or residual analysis.
Parameters a, c, and d in the time-weighting function are undefined and no fit, units, or sensitivity analysis is reported.
Only one time-weight family is studied in depth and the synthetic correlated/uncorrelated experiment omits seeds, sample size, Poisson rate, parameter values, and repeated-run uncertainty.
The validation withholds only the most recent event from two main case datasets rather than using rolling origins, an external set, or repeated cross-validation.
Search Cost tie handling is described only as no preference within the same color, leaving exact rank treatment and color-bin effects unspecified.
Table 1 does not label Search Cost as percent versus fraction and does not state the distance units for Error Distance.
Kernel and time-weight choices are developed and evaluated on the same small case collection, creating tuning and selection optimism.
Time coupling generally worsens the reported values, but the paper offers no statistical test and initially attributes the behavior to bad luck.
The conclusion extrapolates Sutcliffe performance to larger datasets without evidence that more data, different offenders, or different geographies preserve accuracy.
Jack the Ripper dates are printed as 1988 in Appendix A but as 1888 in the preceding date table.
Panel (l) is titled Next Crime Location Probability but its caption calls it a Criminal Location plot.
The page headed Model Plots for Chester Turner actually repeats Sutcliffe coordinates, data, and captions, so the promised Turner visual comparison is absent.
The references contain suspicious pagination, misspellings, and inconsistent bibliographic formatting, limiting reproducibility.

independent_extensions.summary: Normalize spatial weights explicitly and replace raw coordinate geometry with a declared projection or travel-time metric.
Calibrate kernel families and parameters inside nested rolling origins and report field calibration as well as ranking.
Reverse or transform the deviation score consistently, restrict virtual candidates to the interior grid, and sensitivity-test buffer width.
Replace the mislabeled time regression with a correctly indexed baseline and compare multiple fitted survival or interval models.
Use rolling-origin case evaluation with units, tie rules, uncertainty, simple baselines, and case-level abstention diagnostics.
Regenerate every case plot from versioned data and code, add color bars and truth markers, and fail the build on caption-data mismatch.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain decision-contract summaries, limitation-strength pairing, intuition-before-equation, and First-Next-Then procedural prose
retain event-level coordinates and dates while requiring projection, linkage, provenance, chronology, and visual-data integrity checks
retain explicit center, distance, grid, buffer, and metric interfaces while repairing normalization, units, and score direction
distinguish normalized heuristic fields from calibrated probabilities and require direction-consistent transformations
retain modular kernel and time-weight inputs only with explicit parameter calibration and compatibility checks
retain held-out event evaluation while upgrading it to rolling origins, baseline suites, uncertainty, units, ties, and nested tuning
make reliability case-specific and require diagnostics for clustered versus displaced-hub behavior
retain common-coordinate paired heat maps while requiring color bars, truth markers, data-caption checks, and complete case coverage
retain search cost and color-band actions only after units, score direction, capacity, and case applicability are explicit
compare kernels, target types, and coupling modes under one frozen origin, domain, metric, unit, and uncertainty protocol
